# Format Specifications and Syntax

Syntax, grammar, design goals, and versioning status for each format covered
in this research. All claims cite [citations.md](../citations.md).

## TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation)

- **Creator:** Johann Schopplich [16][39]
- **First release:** 2025 [16]
- **Current spec:** v3.0 Working Draft (2025-11-24) [1]
- **License:** MIT [1]
- **Media type:** `text/toon` (provisional, awaiting IANA registration) [1]

### Design Goals

"Compact, human-readable encoding of the JSON data model for LLM prompts" [1].
TOON minimizes token consumption while maintaining lossless JSON
round-trippability [1]. It emerged from a podcast news workflow where the
creator needed to feed structured data to LLMs within constrained context
windows [39].

### Syntax Rules

TOON is **line-oriented and indentation-based** [1]:

- **Objects:** Colon-based key-value pairs with optional type declarations [1]
- **Arrays:** Bracket notation with element count, e.g., `friends[3]: ana,luis,sam` [1]
- **Tabular data:** Header-row declarations like `{id,name,distanceKm}` enable
  compact columnar representation [1]
- **Nesting:** Indentation-based hierarchy, similar to YAML [1]
- **Quoting:** Minimal — strings with special characters or whitespace use
  quotes selectively [1]
- **Encoding:** UTF-8 required [1]

### JSON Compatibility

TOON encodes the JSON data model but its syntax diverges significantly — it is
**not JSON-compatible** and requires dedicated encode/decode tooling [1][12].
The reference implementation (TypeScript) provides `encode()` and `decode()`
functions [16].

## TRON (Token Reduced Object Notation)

- **Creator:** Tim Huang [5]
- **First release:** 2025 [5]
- **License:** MIT [5]
- **Website:** tron-format.github.io (JavaScript SPA; static content does not
  render for web crawlers) [4]

### Design Goals

TRON is a **JSON superset** — any valid JSON is also valid TRON [4][5]. It
adds class/schema definitions to eliminate repetitive property names in uniform
arrays while preserving backward compatibility with JSON parsers for the
non-class portions [5][11].

### Syntax Rules

TRON extends JSON with class syntax [5]:

```
class A: a,b
A(1,2), A(3,4)
```

This replaces the equivalent JSON:
```json
[{"a":1,"b":2},{"a":3,"b":4}]
```
[5]

The class syntax declares a schema once (property names) and instantiates
objects positionally, eliminating key repetition in arrays of uniform
objects [5][11].

### JSON Compatibility

Valid JSON is valid TRON [4][5]. However, TRON's class syntax extensions
cannot be parsed by standard JSON parsers — only the JSON subset is
backward-compatible [11]. A dedicated TRON parser is needed to handle
class definitions [5].

## JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)

- **Creator:** Douglas Crockford [7]
- **First message:** April 2001 (Crockford and Chip Morningstar at State
  Software Inc.) [7]
- **Current standards:** ECMA-404 2nd edition (December 2017) [6], RFC 8259
  (December 2017, STD 90) [7], ISO/IEC 21778 [6]
- **First RFC:** 4627 (July 2006, superseded by 8259) [7]

### Design Goals

"Lightweight text-based syntax for data interchange derived from
ECMAScript" [6]. JSON prioritizes interoperability, simplicity, and
machine-readability over compactness.

### Syntax Rules

Well-known: objects (`{}`), arrays (`[]`), strings (double-quoted), numbers,
booleans, null. Whitespace is insignificant between tokens [6][7].

### Role in Agent Systems

JSON is the **universal baseline** for agent systems. Every major LLM provider
(OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) uses JSON Schema for tool call definitions and
structured output [18][19][33][34]. Constrained decoding on JSON Schema achieves
below 0.1% schema mismatch rate [18].

---

## YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language)

- **Creators:** Clark Evans, Ingy dot Net (Brian Ingerson), Oren Ben-Kiki [8]
- **First release:** 2001 [8]
- **Current spec:** 1.2.2 (October 1, 2021) [8]

### Design Goals

Human-readable data serialization combining elements of XML, C, Python, Perl,
and email (RFC 2822) [8]. Designed primarily for configuration files and data
exchange between languages with different data structures.

### Syntax Rules

Indentation-based, supports mappings, sequences, and scalars. Known
ambiguities include the "Norway problem" (`NO` parsed as boolean false in
YAML 1.1) and type coercion surprises [8].

### Role in Agent Systems

YAML is the primary configuration format for CrewAI (agents.yaml, tasks.yaml)
[36] and is growing in use for prompt templates. Not used for tool call
serialization by any major provider [18][19][33].

---

## XML (Extensible Markup Language)

- **W3C working group:** Chaired by Jon Bosak (Sun Microsystems), 1996 [9]
- **First published:** February 10, 1998 [9]
- **Current spec:** 1.0 Fifth Edition (November 2008) [9]
- **Editors:** Tim Bray, Jean Paoli, C. M. Sperberg-McQueen [9]

### Design Goals

General-purpose markup language for structured documents and data. Tag-based
syntax with explicit semantic boundaries [9].

### Role in Agent Systems

Anthropic explicitly recommends XML tags for structuring Claude prompts,
noting that "Claude was trained to recognize XML tags as prompt-organizing
mechanisms" [20]. Recommended tags include `<instructions>`, `<context>`,
`<document>`, `<example>` [20]. However, XML is used for **prompt structure**,
not for tool call serialization or structured output — all major providers use
JSON Schema for those purposes [18][19][20][33].

## CSV (Comma-Separated Values)

- **RFC:** 4180 (October 2005, informational) [10]
- **Author:** Y. Shafranovich (SolidMatrix Technologies) [10]
- **MIME type:** `text/csv` [10]

### Design Goals

Simple tabular data format with no support for nesting, typing, or
hierarchical structures [10].

### Role in Agent Systems

CSV is the most token-efficient format for flat tabular data — up to 80%
fewer tokens than JSON [11] — but cannot represent nested structures that
agent tool calls commonly require [2][13]. Useful as input context (e.g.,
feeding database results to an LLM) but not for tool call serialization.

## Format Maturity Comparison

| Format | First Published | Current Spec | Standards Body | JSON-Compatible |
|--------|----------------|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| JSON | 2001 | ECMA-404 / RFC 8259 (2017) | Ecma, IETF, ISO | — (baseline) |
| XML | 1998 | 1.0 Fifth Edition (2008) | W3C | No |
| YAML | 2001 | 1.2.2 (2021) | yaml.org | No |
| CSV | 2005 (RFC) | RFC 4180 | IETF (informational) | No |
| TOON | 2025 | v3.0 Working Draft | None | No [1][12] |
| TRON | 2025 | None published | None | Superset [4][5] |

## Gaps and Limitations

- **TRON spec not accessible:** The official site is a JavaScript SPA that
  does not render for static fetching [4]. No standalone spec document was
  found outside the website.
- **TOON spec maturity:** v3.0 is labeled "Working Draft" — it is not a
  released standard [1].
- **No peer-reviewed evaluation of TOON or TRON syntax** exists as of
  April 2026. The JTON paper [12] is the closest independent academic
  evaluation and it tests TOON as a comparison target.
